theory.intro: A **flow network** is a directed weighted graph in which material moves from a start vertex to a finish vertex. The **source** is the vertex everything starts from and the **sink** is the vertex everything ends at.
facts: The **source** is the vertex with no edges directed into it, so everything in the network starts there.
The **sink** is the vertex with no edges directed out of it, so everything in the network ends there.
The **capacity** written on an edge is the largest amount that can move along that edge each time period.
Every edge is directed, so its capacity applies in the direction of the arrow only.
**Outflow** is the amount actually leaving a vertex in each time period. The total capacity of its outgoing edges is an upper limit, not necessarily the outflow.

**Inflow** is the amount actually entering a vertex in each time period. At an intermediate vertex where nothing is stored or added, inflow equals outflow, even if the incoming and outgoing capacities differ.
A **cut** is a line drawn across the network that completely separates the source from the sink.
The **flow capacity** of a network is the total flow through the network. The capacities written on the edges do not tell us the actual flow.
The **maximum flow** is the greatest flow the network can carry from source to sink.

workedExamples.solution_text:
No edge is directed into $K$, so $K$ is the source.
No edge is directed out of $N$, so $N$ is the sink.
Use the arrows, not the positions of the vertices.

At most $23$ L/min can travel from $S$ to $A$.
The arrow allows that direction only.
The $23$ is a capacity, not an actual flow.

Every path from $S$ to $T$ starts with $SA$, $SB$ or $ST$.
The dashed line crosses all three edges.
No path from the source to the sink avoids the line.
The line completely separates the source from the sink, so it is a cut.

The source is $S$ and the sink is $T$.
The line crosses $SE$, $EB$ and $BC$.
Every path from $S$ to $T$ uses $SE$ or $BC$, so every path crosses the line.
The direction of $EB$ does not leave a path that avoids the line.
The source and sink are completely separated, so the line is a cut.

(a) Every path from $S$ to $T$ uses $AT$ or $BT$. The line crosses both edges, so it completely separates source and sink. It is a cut.
(b) The line crosses $AT$, but the path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow T$ avoids it. The source and sink are not completely separated, so it is not a cut.

The line crosses $AC$ and $AD$.
The path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow D \rightarrow T$ avoids the line.
Crossing several edges is not enough: a cut must completely separate the source from the sink.
The dashed line is not a cut.

foundation.solution_text:
No edge is directed into $P$, so nothing arrives there.
No edge is directed out of $V$, so nothing leaves there.
$P$ is the source and $V$ is the sink.

Every path from $S$ to $T$ starts with $SA$, $SB$ or $ST$.
The line crosses all three edges.
It completely separates the source from the sink, so it is a cut.

Every path from $S$ to $T$ finishes with $AT$, $BT$ or $ST$.
The line crosses all three edges.
No path from the source to the sink avoids it, so it is a cut.

The number on an edge is its capacity, not the amount actually flowing.
At most $18$ litres per minute can travel from $A$ to $C$, and because the edge is directed, no water may travel from $C$ to $A$ at all.

The dashed line leaves $S$, $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ on one side and $T$ on the other.
Every path from $S$ to $T$ must finish with $CT$ or $DT$, and both of those edges are crossed by the line.
The line is a cut because it completely separates the source from the sink, so no path from $S$ to $T$ avoids it.

No edge is directed into $K$, so nothing arrives there.
No edge is directed out of $X$, so nothing leaves there.
$K$ is the source and $X$ is the sink.

development.solution_text:
The line crosses $SA$ and $SB$.
The path $S \rightarrow C \rightarrow T$ avoids the line.
The source and sink are not completely separated, so the line is not a cut.

The line crosses $AC$, $BD$, $BC$ and $DA$.
Every path from $S$ to $T$ must cross from the side containing $S$, $A$ and $B$ to the side containing $C$, $D$ and $T$.
The reverse arrow on $DA$ does not provide a path that avoids the line.
The line completely separates the source from the sink, so it is a cut.

The line crosses $AT$ and $BT$, but misses $CT$.
The path $S \rightarrow C \rightarrow T$ avoids it.
A cut must completely separate the source from the sink, so crossing only two of these three edges is not enough.

The dashed line crosses only $AC$ and $AD$.
The path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow D \rightarrow T$ does not cross the line anywhere.
Because a path from $S$ to $T$ still gets through, the line does not separate the source from the sink, so it is not a cut.

The line crosses $CT$ but misses $DT$.
The path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow D \rightarrow T$ avoids the line.
It does not completely separate the source from the sink, so it is not a cut.

Every path from $S$ to $T$ uses $SB$ or $AT$.
The line crosses both edges.
The direction of $BA$ does not leave a path that avoids the line.
The source and sink are completely separated, so the dashed line is a cut.

mastery.solution_text:
The line crosses $BC$ and $DA$ but misses $AC$ and $BD$.
The path $S \rightarrow A \rightarrow C \rightarrow T$ avoids it.
The path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow D \rightarrow T$ also avoids it.
The source and sink are not completely separated, so the line is not a cut.

$C_1$ crosses $PQ$ and $PR$, the two edges leaving the source.
Every path from $P$ to $U$ crosses $C_1$, so it is a cut.
$C_2$ crosses $VU$ but misses $WU$.
The path $P \rightarrow R \rightarrow W \rightarrow U$ avoids $C_2$.
$C_2$ is not a cut because it does not completely separate the source from the sink.

No edge is directed into $F$, and no edge is directed out of $L$.
The dashed line crosses only $GJ$ and $GK$.
The path $F \rightarrow H \rightarrow K \rightarrow L$ crosses the line nowhere.
$F$ is the source and $L$ is the sink. The dashed line is not a cut, because parcels can still travel from $F$ to $L$ through $H$ and $K$ without crossing it.
